name: Mumbai
curation_note: Curated offline by LORE Labs software team for the founder's first real walk tests (Rome remains the commercial launch pack). Focus: South Mumbai's Fort / Kala Ghoda / Colaba / Churchgate heritage area, i.e. the UNESCO 'Victorian Gothic and Art Deco Ensembles of Mumbai' (2018) and Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus (2004), plus a few well-known landmarks further north. Only well-established facts; uncertain claims were left out. review_status=curated: pending `python -m lore_citypack verify` and human editorial review. Coordinates are from memory and approximate (typically within ~30-60 m) - FIELD-CHECK on the first walk and correct before trusting left/right calls.

facts.text: This basalt arch was built to commemorate the landing of King George the Fifth and Queen Mary at Apollo Bunder in December 1911.
It was designed by the architect George Wittet and completed in 1924.
In February 1948, the last British troops to leave independent India marched out through this arch.
Ferries to the Elephanta Caves, a UNESCO World Heritage Site out in the harbour, leave from the jetties beside it.
This equestrian statue honours Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj, the seventeenth-century founder of the Maratha Empire.
It was unveiled in 1961 and faces the Gateway of India across the square.
The Taj Mahal Palace opened in 1903. It was commissioned by the industrialist Jamsetji Tata, founder of the Tata Group.
A popular story says Tata built it after being refused entry to a hotel that admitted only Europeans. Historians debate whether this really happened.
In November 2008 the hotel was one of the targets of the terrorist attacks on Mumbai. It was restored and reopened.
Leopold Cafe on Colaba Causeway was established in 1871 and is one of the city's best-known old cafes.
It features in Gregory David Roberts's novel Shantaram.
It was also attacked during the November 2008 Mumbai attacks; some bullet marks have been left visible on purpose.
The walls of Cafe Mondegar are covered with murals of Bombay life by the cartoonist Mario Miranda.
It is also known for its jukebox, a rarity among Mumbai's cafes.
Colaba was once a separate island. The causeway, completed in 1838, joined Colaba and Old Woman's Island to the main island of Bombay.
Its official name is Shahid Bhagat Singh Road, and its pavements are one long street market.
Regal Cinema opened in 1933 and is one of Mumbai's earliest Art Deco cinemas.
It was designed by Charles Stevens, son of Frederick William Stevens, the architect of the great railway terminus up the road.
This Victorian fountain at Regal Circle was erected in 1865 in honour of the Duke of Wellington.
Before he became famous for defeating Napoleon at Waterloo, Wellington had visited Bombay, in 1801 and 1804.
This Gothic building was built in the 1870s as the Royal Alfred Sailors' Home, named after Prince Alfred, who visited Bombay in 1870.
It was designed by Frederick William Stevens and today houses the headquarters of the Maharashtra Police.
The Mumbai branch of the National Gallery of Modern Art occupies the old Sir Cowasji Jehangir Public Hall.
It opened as a gallery in 1996 and shows modern and contemporary Indian art.
Mumbai's main museum was founded as the Prince of Wales Museum. The future King George the Fifth laid its foundation stone in 1905.
George Wittet, who also designed the Gateway of India, built it in the Indo-Saracenic style, with a dome inspired by Islamic architecture of the Deccan.
During the First World War the building was used as a military hospital, and the museum only opened to the public in 1922.
In 1998 it was renamed after Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj, founder of the Maratha Empire.
Hornbill House is the home of the Bombay Natural History Society, founded in 1883 and one of India's oldest nature research organisations.
The great ornithologist Salim Ali, often called the birdman of India, was closely associated with the society for most of his life.
Jehangir Art Gallery was established in 1952 by Sir Cowasji Jehangir and is one of India's best-known venues for contemporary art.
It is run by a trust and hosts changing exhibitions by Indian artists in several galleries, free to enter.
Kala Ghoda means black horse. The name comes from a black statue of King Edward the Seventh, as Prince of Wales, on horseback, which stood here from 1879.
The royal statue was removed in 1965 and moved to the gardens of the Byculla zoo, Jijamata Udyaan. In 2017 a new statue of a riderless black horse was installed here.
The original statue was a gift to the city from the businessman Sir Albert Sassoon.
Every February since 1999, the Kala Ghoda Arts Festival fills these streets with art, music and talks.
This is India's oldest surviving cast-iron building. Its iron frame was made in England and assembled here in the 1860s.
It was built as Watson's Hotel, and in July 1896 it hosted the first screening in India of the Lumière brothers' films, the start of cinema in India.
Today the building is in poor repair; look at the cast-iron balconies from across the street.
This Gothic library was built between 1867 and 1870 and named after David Sassoon, a Baghdadi Jewish merchant and philanthropist who helped pay for it.
Behind the building is a garden reading room where members read under the trees.
Elphinstone College, one of the oldest colleges in Mumbai, is named after Mountstuart Elphinstone, a governor of Bombay.
B. R. Ambedkar, the principal architect of India's Constitution, studied here.
This sky-blue synagogue was built in 1884 by Jacob Elias Sassoon in memory of his father, Eliyahoo.
It serves Mumbai's Baghdadi Jewish community and was carefully restored in 2019.
Rampart Row takes its name from the ramparts of the old Bombay fort that once ran along here.
Today the street is part of the Kala Ghoda art district, with galleries and cafes in its old buildings.
The Rajabai Clock Tower rises about 85 metres over the University of Mumbai. It was designed by the English architect George Gilbert Scott and completed in 1878.
It was paid for by the stockbroker Premchand Roychand and named after his mother, Rajabai.
Its design is often said to be modelled on Big Ben in London.
A popular story says Rajabai, who was blind, could tell the time for her evening meal from the tower's bells.
The University of Mumbai was founded in 1857, one of the first three modern universities in India, together with Calcutta and Madras.
Its Convocation Hall and library, like the clock tower, were designed by George Gilbert Scott, who never visited India.
The Bombay High Court building was completed in 1878 in the Gothic Revival style, designed by the British engineer James A. Fuller.
The court itself was established in 1862 as one of the three chartered high courts of British India, with Calcutta and Madras.
Look up at the roofline: statues of Justice and Mercy stand above the building.
This open ground is the heart of the UNESCO World Heritage Site of Victorian Gothic and Art Deco Ensembles of Mumbai, inscribed in 2018.
On one side stand nineteenth-century Victorian Gothic public buildings; on the other, a row of 1930s Art Deco apartment buildings. Two eras of architecture face each other across the grass.
On most days the maidan is full of overlapping amateur cricket matches.

pois.name: Art Deco row on the Oval

facts.text: These cream and pastel apartment buildings were built in the 1930s on land reclaimed from the sea in the Backbay reclamation.
Look for the Art Deco details: curved balconies, stepped towers, sunburst motifs and decorative lettering with the building names.
Flora Fountain was built in 1864 and is crowned by a statue of Flora, the Roman goddess of flowers.
It was originally meant to honour Sir Bartle Frere, the governor who pulled down the old fort walls so the city could expand.
The square is now called Hutatma Chowk, Martyrs' Square. Its memorial honours the people killed in the Samyukta Maharashtra movement, which led to the creation of Maharashtra state in 1960.
This circular garden, ringed by uniform arcaded buildings, was laid out in the 1860s as Elphinstone Circle.
It was renamed after Benjamin Horniman, a British editor of the Bombay Chronicle who supported Indian independence.
The Town Hall, with its grand steps and Doric columns, was completed in 1833 in the neoclassical style, designed by Colonel Thomas Cowper.
It houses the Asiatic Society of Mumbai and its historic library.
The library's treasures include a rare fourteenth-century manuscript of Dante's Divine Comedy.
St. Thomas Cathedral opened in 1718 and is the oldest Anglican church in Mumbai.
Churchgate takes its name from it: the gate in the old fort wall that led to this church was called the Church Gate.
This is the home of the Mumbai Samachar, a Gujarati newspaper founded in 1822 by Fardunjee Marzban.
It is widely described as the oldest continuously published newspaper in Asia.
This is the headquarters of the Reserve Bank of India, the country's central bank, which was founded in 1935.
The bank's head office moved here from Calcutta in 1937.
The Bombay Stock Exchange traces its origins to 1875 and is the oldest stock exchange in Asia.
Its tower, Phiroze Jeejeebhoy Towers, stands on Dalal Street, the brokers' street whose name has become shorthand for India's stock market.
Bombay House has been the headquarters of the Tata Group since it was built in 1924.
It was designed by George Wittet, the architect of the Gateway of India.
This district is called Fort because it lay inside the walls of the old British fort of Bombay.
The walls were pulled down in the 1860s under Governor Sir Bartle Frere so the city could grow. Their gates live on in names like Churchgate and Bazargate.
Ballard Estate is a planned business district built in the 1910s by the Bombay Port Trust on land reclaimed from the harbour.
Its uniform stone office buildings were laid out by George Wittet, giving the area a distinctly European, Edwardian look.
Mumbai's General Post Office was completed in 1913, designed by the architect John Begg.
Its great central dome was inspired by the Gol Gumbaz, the seventeenth-century mausoleum at Bijapur.
This railway station was designed by Frederick William Stevens and completed in 1888. It was named Victoria Terminus, for Queen Victoria's Golden Jubilee year of 1887.
It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2004 as an outstanding blend of Victorian Gothic Revival architecture with traditional Indian features.
Look up at the central dome: it is crowned by a statue of a woman representing Progress.
India's first passenger train ran from Bori Bunder, right here, to Thane on the 16th of April, 1853.
The headquarters of the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation, the city government, was completed in 1893.
Like the station opposite, it was designed by Frederick William Stevens, mixing Gothic with Indo-Saracenic elements.
The Bombay Gymkhana sports club was founded in 1875.
Its ground hosted the first Test cricket match ever played in India, between India and England, in December 1933.

pois.name: Sir J. J. School of Art

facts.text: The Sir J. J. School of Art was founded in 1857 with funding from the Parsi philanthropist Sir Jamsetjee Jejeebhoy.
Rudyard Kipling was born in Bombay in 1865, when his father, John Lockwood Kipling, taught here. A bungalow on the campus is known as Kipling House.
Crawford Market was completed in 1869 and named after Arthur Crawford, the city's first municipal commissioner. It is now officially Mahatma Jyotiba Phule Mandai.
The stone reliefs of Indian farmers over the entrances were designed by John Lockwood Kipling, Rudyard Kipling's father.
Metro Cinema opened in 1938. It was built by the Hollywood studio Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer to show its films.
It is one of the landmark Art Deco cinemas of Mumbai.
St. Xavier's College was founded in 1869 by German Jesuits.
Its main building is in the Indo-Gothic style, with pointed arches and a stone courtyard.
Liberty Cinema opened in 1949, soon after Indian independence.
Its interior is one of the best-preserved Art Deco auditoriums in the city.
Eros Cinema opened in 1938. Its cream and red facade is one of the best-known Art Deco buildings in Mumbai.
It was designed by the architect Sohrabji Bhedwar and is part of the UNESCO Art Deco ensemble.
Churchgate station is the southern terminus of the Western line of Mumbai's suburban railway, one of the busiest commuter rail systems in the world.
It is named after the Church Gate of the old fort, which led to St. Thomas Cathedral.
Marine Drive curves for several kilometres along Back Bay. It was built on land reclaimed from the sea in the 1920s and 1930s.
At night its curve of street lights is known as the Queen's Necklace.
The Art Deco apartment buildings along it are part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site inscribed in 2018.
Brabourne Stadium, home of the Cricket Club of India, opened in 1937.
It is named after Lord Brabourne, the governor of Bombay at the time.
Wankhede Stadium opened in 1974. In 2011 India won the Cricket World Cup final here.
Sachin Tendulkar, Mumbai's most famous cricketer, played his final Test match here in 2013.

pois.name: National Centre for the Performing Arts

facts.text: The National Centre for the Performing Arts was founded in 1969 by J. R. D. Tata and Jamshed Bhabha.
It is India's leading venue for Indian classical music, theatre and Western orchestral music, home to the Symphony Orchestra of India.
Officially the Church of St. John the Evangelist, the Afghan Church was built between 1847 and 1858.
It commemorates the British and Indian soldiers who died in the First Anglo-Afghan War, which is how it got its name.
Sassoon Dock was built in 1875 by the Sassoon family and is one of the oldest docks in Mumbai.
It is one of the city's biggest fish markets, run largely by the Koli community, Mumbai's original fishing people. Come at dawn, and expect strong smells.
Chowpatty is the city beach at the north end of Marine Drive, famous for its evening food stalls selling bhelpuri and other street snacks.
During the Ganesh Chaturthi festival, huge processions bring idols of Ganesha here to be immersed in the sea.
The independence leader Bal Gangadhar Tilak was cremated on this beach in 1920.
Mahatma Gandhi stayed in this house whenever he was in Bombay between 1917 and 1934.
It is now a museum and library about Gandhi's life and work.
This ancient water tank, surrounded by temples and steps, was built in 1127 by a minister at the court of the Silhara dynasty.
Legend says an arrow, or baan, shot into the ground during the Ramayana story released a spring of Ganges water here, which gives the tank its name.
This temple is dedicated to Mumba Devi, patron goddess of the Koli fishing community, and the city's name, Mumbai, is widely held to come from her.
The temple was rebuilt on this site in the eighteenth century after the original near Bori Bunder was demolished.
The Haji Ali Dargah is a mosque and Sufi shrine built in 1431 on a small islet off the coast of Worli.
It is reached by a narrow causeway that is covered by the sea at high tide, so visits depend on the tides.
Opened in 1872 as the Victoria and Albert Museum, this is the oldest museum in Mumbai.
Its restoration won a UNESCO Asia-Pacific Heritage Award in 2005.
In the gardens nearby stands the original statue that gave Kala Ghoda its name.
These terraced gardens on Malabar Hill were laid out in the 1880s on top of a reservoir that supplies water to south Mumbai.
They are known for their hedges clipped into animal shapes and for sunset views over Marine Drive.
This seaside temple is dedicated to Mahalakshmi, the goddess of wealth, and is one of the most visited temples in Mumbai.
Legend says the goddess's images were recovered from the sea after a dream, during construction of the Hornby Vellard causeway that joined the islands of Bombay.
This open-air laundry, built in 1890, has rows of concrete wash pens where hundreds of washermen, the dhobis, clean clothes by hand.
The best view is from the road bridge next to Mahalaxmi station.
This temple to Ganesha was first built in 1801 and has grown into one of the most visited temples in Mumbai.
Expect long queues on Tuesdays, the day traditionally associated with Ganesha worship here.
This cable-stayed bridge across Mahim Bay opened in 2009, linking Bandra and Worli over the sea.
Its official name is the Rajiv Gandhi Sea Link.
